title: New Housing Fund Rules: Take What You Can, But Don't Treat It as a Savings Account
dek: The housing fund is not a savings account you can withdraw anytime; fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap — money you should take, you should still take.
why: Three people in different situations — a self-employed worker, a young professional, a property owner — each run their own numbers, turning the 20 clause changes in the new rules into concrete decisions. The second half on flexible-employment contributions and the comparison with the system-inside is especially informative.
who: Employees with a housing fund who aren't sure whether to withdraw or leave it; people considering buying a home, converting a commercial loan to a housing-fund loan, or contributing as a flexible-employment worker; job seekers trying to judge whether a company is well-run.
skip: The opening chat about the show's origin and the three hosts' positions can be fast-forwarded; start from 13:10, when Zhou Yi's experience of using it.

points.h: Six months after auto-withdrawal, I paused it myself
points.body: After Zhou Yi activated Beijing's housing fund no-threshold rental withdrawal of 2000 yuan per month, she found the money slid into another card the moment it arrived, completely decoupled from the mental account for paying rent. By month's end, when her spending card was maxed out, the money was auto-deducted, adding friction to life. After confirming the housing fund balance earns 1.5% interest — higher than the 0.95% one-year bank deposit rate — she paused the withdrawal the next day. Yu Bai noted this contrasts with the advice three years ago to ‘take all you can, use all you can’; two young colleagues in the department had made the same choice. Lao Qian reminded that this is indeed low capital efficiency, but most people can't achieve the efficiency they imagine — people just make fake accounts for themselves.

points.h: The housing fund is not a deposit; not being able to withdraw is the norm
points.body: Yu Bai sketched an extreme scenario: a young person loses their job and goes home with no liquid funds, tens of thousands in the housing fund, but the home is self-occupied — not qualifying for buying or renting. Even if the new rules allow withdrawal for renovation or property fees, if the family has no such needs, they're stuck. If they risk fraudulent withdrawal under false pretenses, they must return the full amount and cannot withdraw any housing fund for three years. So both ‘take all you can’ and ‘treat it as forced savings with a higher rate than a current account’ are valid; it depends on the individual.

points.h: The new rules put renting first in the withdrawal scope
points.body: This revision adjusts 20 clauses. First, renovating a self-occupied home and paying property fees for a self-occupied home are included in the withdrawal scope for the first time; the housing fund no longer serves only loan-based home purchases. Second, previously rental withdrawal required rent to exceed a set proportion of household wage income; this version removes that limit and places renting first in the withdrawal scope. Third, for the first time, flexible-employment workers are formally included in the system: self-employed individuals and part-time workers can voluntarily contribute and apply for housing-fund loans. In addition, the management center should respond to withdrawal applications within three days and loan applications within ten days, and nationwide mutual recognition of contribution records is being advanced.

points.h: The share of housing-fund loans has fallen from 70% to 30%
points.body: Lao Qian's data: this year, the proportion of housing-fund contributions lent out is as low as just over 30%, while at its peak it was over 70% — a steady decline in just a few years. That is, the theoretically most stable, lowest-rate, highest-quality loan channel is actually used by only just over 30% of people. This directly reflects how low the willingness to buy is. Lao Qian also points out the new rules aim at housing consumption, not leverage: renting moved to first place, property fees and renovation can be withdrawn, thresholds greatly lowered — supporting measures as the real estate market shifts from incremental to stock, and also echoing aging: the monthly withdrawal ratio turned up in 2023, exactly when the post-60s generation retired.

points.h: If you want to buy a home, be careful about withdrawing your housing fund
points.body: Yu Bai warns: the housing-fund loan amount is tied to the account balance; in some cities the loanable amount is 16 times the balance, in others 20 times — it varies. Guangzhou also has multiple caps; when applying, the smallest of several standards applies. For example, for a first or second self-occupied home, the minimum down payment is 20%, so a 1 million yuan home can't be loaned more than 800,000; also, monthly repayment exceeding 50% of monthly income is not allowed. So before withdrawing the housing fund as living expenses, check your city's loan rules. Yu Bai is also cautious about the buy logic of ‘rent-to-price ratio close to the housing-fund rate, only a down payment short’: you must also consider depreciation, price fluctuations, and how to withstand risk once a 600,000 down payment is locked up.

points.h: Flexible-employment contributors carry the full amount alone
points.body: For flexible-employment workers, the contribution base and rate are calculated the same as for employees, but there is no employer to pay half — effectively one person bears the full 10% to 24%. The contribution base must be self-declared: declaring below 10,000 yuan requires no proof; above 10,000 yuan requires logging into the individual income tax app to check tax details as documentation, to prevent over-declaring to get a higher loan amount. Zhou Yi calculated: 10,000 yuan at 10% to 24% is 1000 to 2400 yuan, and this money is not counted in individual income tax, but if unused it's a loss. In addition, most pilot cities require continuous contributions for 6 to 12 months before applying for a housing-fund loan, and most do not allow one-time back payments.

points.h: Inside the system, the housing fund is an invisible benefit
points.body: Zhou Yi asked a friend with a public institution job back home; the friend openly showed a screenshot of their housing fund account — monthly deposits were more than double hers, and the balance exceeded her savings. The friend lives at home with no rental need, so the housing fund just accumulates as forced savings or future loan capacity, plus an occupational annuity, and the contribution base includes all bonuses and subsidies. Lao Qian adds: the housing fund is tax-free, and with the individual pension annual cap of 12,000 yuan and a 3% tax on withdrawal, those inside the system get an extra layer of tax advantage. Data: in 2025, the national average annual wage for urban non-private sector employees was 129,441 yuan, for private sector 71,590 yuan — while working hours are the reverse.

points.h: Full housing-fund contributions are a slice for observing a company
points.body: Lao Qian's judgment on ‘is a company that pays the housing fund a more ideal choice’ hasn't changed at all: a company that pays the full housing fund respects employees and respects the rules, meaning it is likely well-regulated in all aspects, not playing cat-and-mouse with policies. He further says this points to not making profit maximization the first goal, treating people as people, and the invisible returns show up elsewhere. Zhou Yi calculated: a wage base of 100, actual take-home just over 70, but the boss pays over 130 — everyone in the chain feels wronged. Lao Qian uses Ford's Model T wage increase as an example — making workers able to afford the car and have time to use it wasn't capitalist conscience, but a better utility function.

A voluntary, fully self-funded supplementary pension system, with an annual cap of 12,000 yuan.

quotes.text: It arrived, but because your phone app has so many notifications, you don't look carefully — like a reminder that 2000 yuan came in, and it just sits in that card until the end of the month, when my spending card is maxed out and it gets auto-deducted from that card.
But the fact is people make fake accounts for themselves, people withdraw on impulse for all sorts of reasons, people are very good at self-deception.
You really can't treat the housing fund as a deposit, because your bank deposit you can withdraw anytime, but the housing fund you can't.
And it's the highest-quality loan channel, the rate is so low, but only just over 30% of people took loans — at the peak it was over 70% — in just a few years.
I think a company that pays the full housing fund shows it respects employees and respects the rules.

Treating people as people doesn't mean increasing costs; it also means one person's spending — the household sector's spending — becomes the corporate sector's income, and the corporate sector's spending becomes the household sector's wages. These two are a virtuous cycle.
Take all you can, use all you can — buying a home, building, renovating, repaying loans, renting, retirement, leaving the country — all can use it.
